The decision as such, having read it, seems to be that there are serious reasons to believe that Mr. Lazarevic - serious enough to make him stand trial - serious reasons to believe that he may have been involved in fraud for the amounts we find in this document. What else would you like to establish?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me, on page 30, and I believe that's page 33 in English, where he states: "In the end, in January of 1995" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to his statement. In B/C/S, that's page 30; and in English, I believe it is page 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we are now looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are looking at his statement of 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is not in evidence, Mr. Bakrac. So don't ask us to look at anything which is not before us yet. But tell me what he states there, and then I'll further listen to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It states there, Your Honour, his words: "In the end, in January 1999, I fled the SRY." Now, if you take a look at that time-period, the fraud that he committed was in the period between September and December 1998. And in January 1999, as he himself states, he fled the SRY, FRY, and then from January, for six months, he had this exchange with the Prosecutors. I will not insist on many of the facts. I will just point out the indictment to him, ask him about it. They're people mentioned there, in the indictment, the contract numbers with these people that he actually entered into. And I will just ask him whether he actually entered into a contract with these individuals. That would be sufficient. And in the Milosevic case when he was confronted with this when he was asked whether he actually engaged in fraud in 1998, he said that he didn't but added that he had left Serbia a very comfortable life, where he had a Porsche and a Mercedes vehicle, and left the country for political reasons. So I believe this is very relevant. And please trust me, I will not burden you with all of the documents that have I entered into the e-court but will just restrict my questions to a few documents just do show the MO of this witness which can perhaps be helpful for determining what kinds of person this witness is and his character.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you assist me in giving me the date and the page numbers in the Milosevic so that I can re-read them during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, gladly. Just bear with me a moment, please. That's 12683 and 12684. This was in the re-examination by my learned friend Groome when he was asked whether he had actually been given some money for cooperation or gained any benefits from it. Then he said that he had had a much better life in Belgrade, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking for the page references and date references. I received the page, not yet the date. Is that 29th, 30th, or 31st.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 31st, Your Honours. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 31st of October, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stanisic, I do not feel very comfortable in having made this session longer than I intended to do. Apologies for that. We'll resume at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, it will be Mr. Bakrac who will now cross-examine you. He is also going to make breaks, although it's easier because he will speak his own language and you're speaking -- well, I do not know whether I should say your own language, whether you consider English your own language or not. But, again, try to slow down and make those breaks. Mr. Bakrac, please proceed. Mr. Bakrac, by the way, is counsel for Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. May I just take this opportunity to advise the Chamber that for the first time today we have our new Case Manager, in the courtroom. Mr. Vulic Bozidar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell me what you would prefer me to address with you? Mr. Lazarevic or Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have been warned by His Honour, Judge Orie. It really makes no difference, so go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is very kind what Mr. Bakrac does.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I was going to suggest that you provide your answers in English so that we may avoid the overlapping, so I will now begin. Would you please take a look at your statement provided to the Office of the Prosecutor between January 1st and July 1st, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please pull up page 1 of this statement, both in English and in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And not to be shown to the public. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Witness, I will put my question to you while we wait for the statement to come up on the monitor, and then you will actually be able to actually see it and read it. You said that you were born in 1947 and that in 1956 you moved to Sarajevo and that you studied languages and graduated from the Sarajevo University in 1968. You -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's not really Sarajevo University. It is philosophy. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, one more thing: I would appeal to you - please don't misunderstand me - but I would like to tell you that our time is restricted, so, please, just restrict your answers to the questions that I pose to you. Now, your father was employed by the so-called UDBA; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And he was the one who actually introduced you to Mr. Zimonja, who worked for KOS, for the army, the counter-intelligence service of the army; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My question is this: Yesterday you tried to describe, in a cute sort of way, the level of frictions and -- frictions between these two services. You said this could be compared to a football match between Partizan and the Red Star one of them being, in this case the -- the army would be the UDBA and the Red Star -- the army would be Crvena Zvezda and the other one would be the Partizan. Now tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the last part of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part of your question, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The last portion of my question related to this: How come that your father, who was an UDBA employee, did not actually introduce you to someone from UDBA so that you could work for them, but, rather, he introduced you for -- with someone or to someone from the army? And you said yesterday that there were frictions between these two services.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain that. Why -- what was the decision behind it, but, you know, that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood the next paragraph from your statement correctly, you said, in paragraph 2 on page 1, in the very first line: "The first task that Zimonja gave me was to infiltrate student groups at Sarajevo University, which, in 1968 were involved in unrests. He also tasked me with keeping an eye on foreigners in Sarajevo. This was supposed to be accomplished by my arranging chance meetings with them." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Which foreigners in Sarajevo were you referring to when you said that? Did you mean the foreign students or some other foreigners?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the other foreigners, not students.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you provide an example. In 1968, in Sarajevo, what foreigners were there and what kind of positions were they in?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of eastern Germans, if I remember correctly. There were a few French, a few Brits. And the positions, I don't know, it was just to kind of arrange a chance meeting with them, help them out, try to get close to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But you being an intelligence officer who is supposed to approach them and assist them, offer your assistance, you were supposed to also know what kind of job or what kind of work these people were doing; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the very, very early beginning of my career as an intelligence officer, so I don't think I was ever informed about a particular -- about a certain -- I was never given a task of an individual that I'm going to follow that person, that he does that and that and we want to know more about him. It was just establishing the contact and we see how we go from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And if I understood your answer correctly, since you didn't know anything else about them, you would just establish contact with them, say, Hello, I'm so-and-so, and what's your name and -- so what kind of report would you then send?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it didn't go exactly like that. It would be more a situation which obviously the foreigner needed some assistance, whether it's in a store buying a souvenir or trying to buy an ice-cream, he can't explain; things like that. And the initial report? There wouldn't be any unless the situation developed in that direction that it needed a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, you would send the report to Zimonja, saying a German bought an ice-cream cone in an ice-cream shop; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please put serious questions to the witness, Mr. Bakrac. Until now, none of the questions the Chamber was able to detect what the relevance was. If you would first put the question -- questions to the witness where it is clear to the Chamber what the relevance is, and if there is then any time left, you can ask questions about ice-creams. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, in 1969, you said you served in the military, the compulsory military service for 18 months, in Kraljevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you also say I was assigned -- I had contact with KOS officers at the barracks where I was posted, but they never asked me to do any work on behalf of KOS during my army service. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing they asked me at the time was to supply all the name and addresses of people that are living overseas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So in 1969, while you were serving in the army, you were asked to provide addresses of people who lived abroad? Which people? Soldiers? Which people living abroad?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. And already then, even before you went to serve your military service, you had established contact with Mr. Nikola Zimonja; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: All right then. Now I would like to show you an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please pull up P265, or, rather, 65 ter document 265.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Although we did receive about 55 documents from the Defence, unless I'm mistaken, I do not think that 65 ter 265 was on that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it was on the list that the Prosecutor was going to use during their examination, and that is the reason why I did not put it on my list. It is true that, at the last moment, the Prosecutor actually removed six of the documents from their list, but I don't think this one was among them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, I find on the list of the Prosecution and -- those exhibited, 262 and 266. Any further problems in dealing with the document? If it was once on your list, then I take it that you have looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we have no problem with the Defence counsel using it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then you could even have refrained from making this observation if it previously was on your list, Ms. Marcus. Something to think over for the next time. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, do you recognise this military ID? It says it's a duplicate but I see it bears no photo or signature. Is this perhaps one of the documents that you handed over to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page, please, where we can see all the information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the document that I gave, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Lazarevic, my first question is the following: Is it common for a document of this type to be left without a photograph and without the signature and not to bear a stamp over the -- the photo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I wouldn't know. That's how it was given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. Now, Mr. Lazarevic, could you take a look now at page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page in e-court, please. Could we have the next page on the screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It says here, Mr. Lazarevic, actually it shows the dates when you actually were in the army serving; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1966 to 1969? I can't see it really, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it says from the 29th of September, 1966, to 12 February 1968. You've just told us that in 1968 you met Mr. Zimonja and that you went to serve your compulsory military service in 1969. Now tell me, which of the two is true? Is this document falsified, or was what you said true and this document counterfeit, or is it possible that you met Mr. Zimonja before 1966, when you were 17?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is a correct date which is in Vojnak Uzice [phoen], which is a duplicate. So that is correct. So the 1968 I did met Zimonja -- well, I actually finished my military service before 1968, end of the 1968. 1966 to 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How, then, was it possible that you would be assigned tasks from KOS in the army? You told us a moment ago that, first, you met Zimonja, then you went to serve in the military, and then you were assigned a task to actually monitor the movement of foreigners. But now you told us that you met Zimonja after you've completed your military service. So which of the two is actually true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is that I have done my military service but I, for some reason, misjudged the year that I was giving to the Prosecution. But this is a genuine document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, the problem is not in the years, Mr. Lazarevic, but, rather, in your activities. There is no issue here with the years. You said that first you met Zimonja, then you went to serve in the army, and then you were given some tasks by KOS to provide some names of some foreigners. And now, five minutes later, you're telling us, No, I actually met Zimonja after I served in the army. So you actually concocted this whole story that you were given a task to provide names of foreigners while you were serving in the army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. This is just a simple genuine mistake about give the date which happens, I don't know, some 30 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, a mistake in a date is that you say whether it was in 1968 or 1967. However, what you did first and what you did after that is a matter of sequence of events. Therefore, it's more than just a mistake on a date. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will no longer insist on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, after you completed military service, you returned to Sarajevo and you were -- you got employed at the department store Nama; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What kind of work did you do there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Some clerical job, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you send reports to Nikola Zimonja at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I had nothing to send, I didn't send anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then out of the blue, according to your statement, on page 1, you say: "The first big assignment I got was to plant some films on a German tourist who was camping on the coast." So all of a sudden Zimonja came up with these tapes and he said, Plant them on a German tourist who was camping on the coast. Is that true? That's what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true, but I wouldn't call it suddenly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, you said that you worked at Nama department store, that you hadn't been given any task or assignment, that you were trying again to arrange some chance meetings with foreigners who were staying at hotel Evropa, and you tried to establish contact with them in the neighbourhood of this hotel. We've already discussed this. And then you said: "The first big assignment was ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, are you quoting from a statement which is not in evidence. I'd like to see that on the screen so to be able to follow what you're putting to the witness. Could we please have the statement, not to be shown to the public, but at least in e-court on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I have this nagging fear that I will inadvertently disclose something to the public. But could we see, then, page 1 of the statement. It is the last paragraph on page 1 -- or, rather, page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: There, now you can see it in English. And since you are giving your answers in English, now everyone will be able to follow what we're saying. So you said: "The first big assignment I got was to plant some films on a German tourist who was camping on coast. I received the the films from Zimonja and then I travelled to the island of Rab." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now do you know what -- what kind of footage it was? What was depicted in those films?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you interested in the contents of the films?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps get -- could you perhaps imagine that this man on whom you were planting these films could, in some situations, be accused of a very serious criminal offence of intelligence collection? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Uh-huh. No, so you weren't aware of this. Why, then, do you go on to say: "To be honest, at the time, the whole thing was very appealing and exciting to me, and I didn't give much thought to what kind of consequences this German might have." So what did you mean there by consequences for the German?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only assume, but I would not have any exact reasoning for it, what would happen to him, nor did I think about it. And, of course, I was excited. I was a young man. I saw myself -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But you could imagine that some serious consequences might ensue for this man?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't think of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wasn't the question, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you could imagine, not whether you did. I mean, if you plant some material on another person, he may face the negative consequences of an untruthful created situation. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour. I agree with you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And may I take it that being young and being excited that you were still aware that planting somewhere, something, which wasn't there originally, could do harm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I actually thought about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were not thinking at all at the time or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was thinking I'm doing a favour to somebody in my own country; I'm doing it against a person that I dislike intensely, being a German. I was thinking along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So based on your answers that you're providing now, Mr. Lazarevic, may I claim that even to this day, even today, here, as you speak, although you're aware that you might cause harm to these two accused, you are still putting forward a whole series of untruths that could be hurtful to them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bakrac, could you please split up this question because there is an unexpressed suggestion in your question that the witness is now giving false testimony as he, at the time, did implant false evidence in a situation. If you want to put that to the witness, fine. But then do it explicitly, and not somewhere hidden in a question. So, therefore, you may rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, that was not my intention. I didn't mean to hide anything. But based on the statement provided by this witness and his answers to your and my questions, I have concluded - and this is what I'm proposing to the witness - that even today he is trying to plant things on other people, that he's telling untruths without thinking of the possible consequences of those untruths for these two accused here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So is that correct, Mr. Lazarevic? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I absolutely disagree with you. You're drawing a line between something that happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This doesn't need any further explanation. If the witness says that this is not true, I take it that he says he is not lying at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore it's not -- whether -- the Chamber will, at a later stage, will, of course, evaluate all the evidence in this case, including the evidence of, Mr. Lazarevic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, after this episode with the Germans and according to your statement that's - and that's on page 2 in English and page 3 in B/C/S - you left for England where you were assigned the task of monitoring or observing the Serbian emigré circles in England. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When did you go to England, and who gave you this assignment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would really have to look at the passport when I entered England. At this particular moment in time, I can't remember. But it's in my passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Approximately, can you remember the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How long were you in London for?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 18 months, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: All right, sir. Can you please look at your statement now. Can you look at page 3 in the B/C/S and 2 in the English. In paragraph 2 you say - let me not lose time to read all about your work in London - but you say this lasted for about nine months but then they told me that they wanted me to go to Australia. Nine months and 18 months is very different, even from this point in time, looking back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually this is on page 3 in the English, I apologise. In the English version it's page 3, paragraph -- exactly in the middle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, if you had my passport in your hand, and you have seen what time I left, what time I arrived Dover, and what time I left London to go back to France, you're asking me now suddenly to remember how long I stayed, and you already know? It's an unfair question because I already told you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you're not invited to comment on the way in which you're cross-examined. You're invited to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you have an explanation for the fact that you once stated nine months to have been in England and why you now state that it was 18 months.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was nine months. Right now, the first number that came to my head was 18, so I said 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you perhaps not immediately express what comes to your mind by verify internally as well the accuracy of what comes to your mind. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: After that, KOS ordered you to go to Australia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How did they do that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through Yugoslav Club in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was there a particular person who came to you and told you that you were to go to Australia and explain to you why you needed to do that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not a particular man. There was a message left for me to get in touch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yet in touch with whom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Get in touch with Zimonja where?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as possible. By a telephone, or in person, or however. I believe I spoke on the phone to him, if I remember correctly again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what did he tell you then, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember he said something to do with a bunch of Croatian emigrés arriving from Australia into former Yugoslavia, entering at the border with Austria, being followed along the terrain there, and they more or less shot everybody except one guy, and he gave him information that they are actually from Woolongong area in Victoria, Australia. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then you went there. Did he give you a direct order to go there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember his direct order, but it was a suggestion that might be a good thing if could I get there and there was no reason why I couldn't. I didn't have any obligations to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Excellent. Who financed your trip to Australia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Australian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On what grounds did it finance your trip to Australia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immigration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps work for their service?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I just filed an application for immigration to Australia. Once it was approved, the ticket was paid for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. And then when you came to Australia, to Woolongong, if I'm pronouncing the name of the town correctly, where did you get a job?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A local bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what did you do in the local bank?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Administrative work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you do any kind of espionage assignments in the bank at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they might have asked me to check what is the financial status of some of the Yugoslavs living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is that something that you think, or you are asserting that? Is that something that you are sure that they asked you to do or you are not sure that they asked to you do?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure. I'm pretty sure they asked me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who asked you to do that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people that sent me to Australia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You just said that you went to Australia at the expense of the Australian government, as an immigrant, and that Zimonja just made a suggestion that you should go to Australia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all had to do with building a cover when I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who did you report to when you arrived Australia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it was again done through Yugoslav Embassy, or consulate, or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm going to read back to you your statement on page 3, both in the English and B/C/S version, where you say: "Shortly after my arrival in Sydney, I was taken by members of the Yugoslav Embassy staff to a house where they briefed me about my work in Australia." Then you go on. So Yugoslav Embassy staff in Australia knew that you were a KOS agent. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What is the basis for your assumption?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way they dealt with me was just as a young Yugoslav agent who came in as immigrant and is willing to continue to work for the Yugoslav government.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And did you continue your contacts with Zimonja through the Yugoslav Embassy in Australia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On and off.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your testimony to date you just said that Zimonja was the only one who knew that you were in KOS and that Zimonja was the only one you knew, had something happened to Zimonja you would not have known whom to get in touch with. Is that not what you previously stated?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did state that previously, but it was more as a thinking about a joke than anything else. Of course I'd know who to get in touch with, if I needed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. You said that you were supposed to monitor the financial situation of Serb emigrés. How would you be able to establish who had how much money in their accounts? Can you explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you worked in a bank, you have the name of the clients, you can enter the accounts and see what the status is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Using a computer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said you can physically go and look it up. I didn't ever mention a computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And so you did have the possibility physically to look at the account number of each one of our citizens and see exactly how much money was on that account; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- not necessarily that way that you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How then? Can you explain it to us, please. How did you actually implement the assignment that you were given and because of which you had come to Australia? That is, how could you see how much was on these accounts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be given the name of the person to check on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who would you receive this name from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who sent me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then you would freely, without any problems, be able to access that account, as a bank employee?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And this data about the money, how many people did you compile this data for?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you. After that, you were given an assignment to join the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: -- painters and port dockers workers union.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, from what I read in your statement, you did this job for approximately one year. Now, you must have an idea on how many persons you were asked to check on their financial situation. Was this a weekly event? Was it three times a week? Was it once a month? You must have some recollection to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will tell you. First the thing that I discovered that Woolongong itself is predominantly Macedonian population there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not asking for such details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I want you to focus on whether this was a monthly event. You said you got names and you were to check on persons. The question simply was: How often did you do that? Now, if you have worked there for a year, it's difficult to understand that you say, No idea.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, that I remember, the closest number I can come up with is about 20 to 25, that is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would mean twice a month, approximately. Is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was not originally given all the names at the same time and given a period of time to find out; I might have been given a name this week, a month down the road another name, and so on. But I'd say, in total, over a year, I don't think it was more than 25 to 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So do know an answer to that question. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would have a whole series of questions but because my time is limited, I'm not going to dwell on this anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: After this, you were told to join the painters and dockers union. Is that your next assignment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my next assignment, but it was not suggested. It was my option.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That was your option then. I'm now going to read to you what you told the investigators of the Prosecutor's office. "After I left the job at the bank, I went to work at a steel mill, an enterprise which employed a large number of Yugoslavs, all of whom were affiliated with the painters and dockers union. This organisation was extremely powerful. And because its members was employed in a number of key industries" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, when reading, your speed of speech goes up. So try to read slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this excerpt is on page 4 of the English version, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not going to go back and lose time. Have you found what I have just been reading so that I can continue? "This organisation was extremely powerful. And because its members were employed in a number of key industries, this union had the ability to effectively shut down Australia with a strike. Also, the union, at the time, was providing funds to the Irish Republican Army. The Yugoslav government was interested in this aspect since they were supplying weapons to the IRA." You yourself thus decided to go or you were given the assignment. Well, let's let that be my first question. The dockers and painters union with Serb members was able to paralyse or shut down Australia with a strike and it also financed the IRA. Can you please explain how exactly this worked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could we, at the same time, have the next page in English on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, we don't have a lot of time, and I have a lot of questions for you, so kindly, would you, please --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was your last question? Because there are some similarity. I never claimed that the painters and dockers union was a Serbian union. When did I say that? There were some Serbs working within the docks of Sydney, and it was a very strong union, but it is a predominantly Australian union, not Serbian union.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say that this was a company which employed a large number of Yugoslavs, all of whom were affiliated with the painters and dockers union. Is this not correct? You can see for yourself what your statement says in English. Does that reflect what you yourself told the Prosecutor's office or not? Can you please look at that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find out which paragraph you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the last paragraph on the page which is in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The first line is totally incorrect. I did work at the steel works. The steel works does not belong to the painters and dockers union. They're a different union all together. But I did go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's -- What do you want to know, Mr. Bakrac? I can imagine that one of the things you'd like to know is why Mr. Lazarevic told us that it was his option to go there, it was not suggested to him. Let's try to get to the core of what you apparently want to know. Please put a clear question in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is sufficient. We're losing too much time. I have a lot of questions. I'm not going dwell on this. I'm now just going to complete this KOS period of work with one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, can you please look at page 4 in the Serbian, in the B/C/S, and page 4 in the English, please. I am going to slowly read it to you. "In that period, I moved around some, working as an interpreter. I did not like Australia, and I bore a grudge against my handlers for sending me there in the first place." Well, let us stop there. Then in the statement you say that they sent you, whereas earlier you said that this was your decision. What is true of these two things?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said it was my decision to go to Australia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. Then I misunderstood you, Mr. Lazarevic. Then you go on to say: "These feelings had been compounded in 1975 when my mother died. She had been sick with cancer for several months and was hospitalised for some period, KOS was, of course, aware of this, yet they did not tell me anything. I was informed of her death three months after she died. This caused me, for the first time, to really feel disillusioned with them." Mr. Lazarevic, were you on some kind of covert assignment so secret that you were not able to contact your family in Yugoslavia and that KOS, three months after the death of your mother - and I'm sorry; I regret having to ask you about this unfortunate affair - but it is very strange to me that you would be on such a secret assignment that you would be unable to be in contact with your family so that it was necessary for KOS to let you know three months after the fact that your mother had died?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. I mean, at my age, I would send a letter once a month and maybe get a reply to it in a month from my mother. She lived alone. And if I didn't get a letter in two months, I didn't much about it. But do you know how -- do you know how I got informed about it? Would you like to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, no. Sir, Mr. Lazarevic, your mother did not have a telephone.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she didn't have telephone, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did she live? I'm sorry for having to ask. Where did she live?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In an apartment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And she didn't have a telephone. All right. Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic, you keep referring in your statement, and I'm going finish here with your work as a KOS agent, you keep referring to what KOS is. And can you please tell me what KOS means, and what is the actual correct name of that service that you were working for?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general name that everybody used was Kontraobavesajna Sluzba. Their real name: Kontraobavesajna Grupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And I assert that that is not the correct answer. In the Yugoslav People's Army, what is the correct name of that organ; do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, it was KOS and always will be KOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, when you testified in the Milosevic case, Witness Candic testified after you. Mustafa Candic, he's not a protected witness; I can refer to him. I have the page and the reference and everything. He explained, because he worked in the air force intelligence service, he explained that KOS, K-O-S, it's actually a name that actually stayed among the public from Second World War; whereas now you're stating that it was always KOS and that is -- but actually it's only the name that the service is known by amongst the people. But those who actually worked in the service know what the correct name of the service is. I'm going to tell you now. Did you have a KOS in your brigade, the 21st Krajina Brigade -- actually, in the 21st Corps? Did you have a KOS in the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from myself, I don't know. There are a lot of colonels there, but they all claim that they are internal security. [B/C/S spoken]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the correct name, the security organ or the security administration, and do you know the structure of the security administration along the vertical line?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a uniformed officer of the JNA, apart from serving national service. So my knowledge is probably very limited about the vertical structure of organs within the army. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [In English] Fair enough. [Interpretation] Fair enough. I'm not going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'm trying to understand your questions and the answer. You put to the witness, you say, KOS, that's not the proper name. Then the witness suggests something else with Grupa at the end, and then you say, That's not the correct answer. Fine. Then you go on and you continue by asking, Was there KOS in your 21st - what was it? - did you have a KOS in the 21st -- it reads corps, but ... Now, what, then, should the Chamber understand this to be? KOS isn't the proper name? The name given by the witness is not the correct name? Then you're asking about the KOS -- what is, then, that question? Why not put to the witness apparently what -- what you consider to be the right name? You ask him, Was it KOS? Or perhaps official name was different. You say that's inaccurate. Then it -- the evidence flows away. Where the Chamber is interested to know what apparently you're putting to this witness, that he is not giving the right answers. Then give him the name as you understand it to be and say, Does this refresh your memory? Then we know what we are talking about. But, at this moment, at least I - I cannot speak for my colleagues, but they will kick me under the table if I am wrong - I get lost in this, if I may say, in this little chaos. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand you completely, and I understand where my error is. But my error is time related. This is a very important witness for us, and, really -- well, it's like this. I am -- like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I am asserting, and it exists here, let's say the command of the 24th Brigade, then the security organ, so the top -- the highest instance in the military that you claim you worked for for 30 years is called the security administration; whereas the lower units are security organs and security groups. This is what I am asserting and putting to you: That you don't even know the name of the service that you allegedly worked for for 30 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wanted to ask counsel if we could know when he quotes something. It appeared he was quoting something. I'm not sure if he was. But if he was, maybe we could know what he is quoting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he consulted his notes, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just looked at my notes because there are thousands of documents where the security organ is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is put to you, Mr. Lazarevic, what the proper names were of the -- of the security organs. Top, highest instance, security administration; at the lower level, security organs and security groups. That's what is put to you. Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not how I see it. When Mr. Bakrac is talking about security organs, to my mind springs security, internal, leaning with security of the corps, it's brigades, this is not what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're saying --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I worked for KOS. Name KOS is well known. Stayed with me all my life. If they changed it sometimes during their history, I don't know. And I claim again: I was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. Your explanation simply is that what Mr. Bakrac is referring to may be internal security organs or elements or whatever you would call it, and that's not you were working for, and that's not what you are referring to. Is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please, next question, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I ask for a very very short break, like for five minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we will even have a longer break. And I already will allow you to leave the courtroom. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Lazarevic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Back in five?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, we will have the normal break now. So you will have some 25 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, in your cross-examination you have to make up your mind. What my experience is until now is that you started with a few questions of which the relevance was totally unclear, not only to me but to my colleagues as well, and then you entered in some areas and always halfway, when the confusion was complete, you said, I've no further time for this; I will move on to my next item. That is not assisting the Chamber very much. You have to select the most important items of your cross-examination and then to explore them at a level so that we can learn something from it, that the witness is not telling the truth, or that he is distorting the truth, whatever. But to take it halfway, leave us with a lot of uncertainties which then are not resolved in any way, is -- and then to say, Well, I haven't got much more time, that is not really -- I can imagine, for example, that if you're talking about a passport, when he entered into England, that you would have explored that further and that you would have that passport or whatever. But to come to a conclusion on matters you are touching upon, that's what really would assist the Chamber. Would you please keep that in mind for the time to come. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Could we now pull up Exhibit 2D58 in e-court. And while we wait for it to appear, let me just say that it was a document that was disclosed to us under Rule 68 from -- by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And I would ask the witness to take a look at this document and tell us if he recognises it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us wait for a moment to have the English version on the screens as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, since we can see both versions, both the English and the B/C/S versions on the screens, could you please tell us, after looking at it carefully, tell us, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see my signature on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Your signature is missing there. We received this document from the Prosecutor. And my question for you is: Do you recognise this document or not? That's all. As enclosure it says short curriculum vitae and then, above that, Topusko, 28th of April, 1992, respectfully Slobodan Lazarevic, Topusko, no signature. I agree. So my question to you is: Did you actually type this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, to be perfectly honest with you. I really do not remember this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You do not remember a significant thing such as this, that on the 28th of April, 1992, you requested the proper body in the command to take -- to accept your application in view of the fact that you were employed as a volunteer in the 8th Organisational Group as a communications officer with the ECMM and UNPROFOR since 17th January and so on and so forth. So you can't remember that you actually sent a document of this nature, together with your resume?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a distinct possibility, but I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since the witness admits that this might be a document that he authored, I would like to tender it into document -- into evidence. And also, something that I actually omitted earlier, that military ID, to be admitted into evidence. So first could we please have document 2D265 admitted and then this one, 2D58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just query whether the witness has authenticated the document. That's -- that's our submission. If the witness can authenticate the document, then we would have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if he cannot?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If he cannot, then perhaps there's another basis for authentication. Or maybe the -- if the counsel would like to tender it from the Bar table, then I suppose -- just a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps, for the moment, with your leave, it could be marked for identification, if anything, so that we could have a moment to look into it a little more deeply. It's one of numerous documents that we received just last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But isn't it true that Mr. Bakrac told us that he received this document from you under Rule 68? And now 68 is an unclear reference to whether it's 68(i) or 68(ii). Is this the relevant document or is it exculpatory? How was it presented to you, Mr. Bakrac? A reference to Rule 68 is not -- makes quite a difference --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, from what I could see, all it states there is under Rule 68. Now, you know I don't want to repeat here the circumstances under which we actually began to work on this case, but if you allow me a moment, I will try and research this a bit further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Groome has an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't answer that question. But we received 54 documents trying to figure out what we can about these documents. There is a note in the file that may have received this document from the witness himself. I'm trying to confirm that now. Obviously we have no objection if the document were received from the witness himself. I'm in the middle of trying to determine that at the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be marked for identification, and the parties are invited to make further submissions as to its origin or whatever information could shed light on the authenticity of the document. So for the Chamber to further consider whether it will request authentication of this document. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D19, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. It will keep its status for the time being. Then the military ID? Any objections against ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: None. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D20, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I can be of assistance, my colleague just informed me that this document was disclosed under Rule 68. It doesn't cite the subparagraph exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, apparently from the words of the Prosecution, it needs to be explored in more detail. I've given a ruling. Submissions are invited. Not at this moment, orally, to be made. But to file them as soon as possible. D20 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I also requested the military ID that I had confronted the witness with, to tender it into evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you did so. I ruled on it already, after it had been given number D20. If would you please keep alert of what happens in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. And I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I would now like to move on to your employment, or, rather, engagement, at the 21st Corps, the Krajina Corps. First of all, please tell us when was the 21st Corps, better known as the Kordun Corps, established?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shortly prior to withdrawal of the JNA troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say that, could you tell us more specifically approximately the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Up until March 1992, where were you employed, or, rather, where were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interpreter to General Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, tell me, please, who was the commander of the 21st Corps from the time it was established, as you said, in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Bulat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm now in possession of information related to D19 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I earlier said that we'd now like to further hear the evidence of this witness. I said the Chamber invites you to make submissions. And I explained to Mr. Bakrac that we'd like to receive written submissions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we now please pull up in e-court Exhibit 2D38.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This is a brief certificate or receipt, Mr. Lazarevic. Please take a look at this certificate. We will see the English version in a moment. Right now, we just have the B/C/S. Could you please tell us or explain to us what this is. What do we see in front of us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This piece of document was given to me by Colonel Bulat in Belgrade upon our return to Belgrade. And it was just a certificate of the time which I spent within the 21st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When did Mr. Cedomir Bulat give this to you in Belgrade? What year?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: End of 1995, beginning of 1996. Thereabouts. I don't really remember. It was supposed to be a document as a proof which will be entered --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, is this document, this certificate, was it filed anywhere? Can you see the filing number or stamp? Was it ever filed anywhere, at any institution?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that in a moment. So we see here that you spent, as a member of the 21st Krajina Corps on the front line from the 21st of December, 1991, through August 14th, 1995, and you just told us a moment ago that you were with the Krajina Corps since March 1992. So which is more correct? What you told us today or what we can see in the certificate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 21st of December, Kordun Corps was not in existence. I think it got formed February or March 1992. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Unless I misunderstood, I believe that counsel has misquoted what the prior answer was in terms of March 1992. The question was about when the 21st Corps was established, and, to that, the witness replied March 1992. So I just want to know what he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that change anything to the issue at stake? That is that when the witness says it was established that, of course, we could not expect him to be a member of a unit which has not yet been established, would we? So, therefore, it comes down to the same. And what Mr. Bakrac is doing is to put to the witness that he said that it was established in, I think he said late March, just prior to the withdrawal of the JNA, whereas we find here a document saying that he served on this unit, the Krajina Corps, since 21st of December. That's the issue. And that doesn't -- I think your intervention -- again, I agree with you, that literally you're right; but if there's any substance in it, I would like to know what it is, because I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I withdraw the objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Lazarevic, could you please explain the discrepancy and which is true; what you told us a moment ago or what we can read in this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I read this document, it becomes very clear what happened here. The date of 21st of December, 1991, is the day I arrived in Krajina, and it was the day I arrived. This is not the date when the corps was formed. Now, Colonel Bulat, in his wisdom or whatever the reason was, he chose to use the date of my arrival on territory of RSK as a starting working for the 21st Corps, even though the 21st Corps, as such, did not exist at the time. And this document was written after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Excellent, Mr. Lazarevic. My next question is this: Is it correct that it says there Commander Colonel Cedo Bulat, and then there's a stamp affixed, reading -- the stamp, the 40th Personnel Centre Command? Am I reading this correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably you are. But I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, trust me. That's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, since you said, So, my question is this: When was Colonel Bulat the commander of the 44th [as interpreted] Personnel Centre in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I didn't even look at the stamp to be perfectly honest with you. But I got it, I mean, I didn't look at. Because everybody was going to the building where the government in exile was, including Colonel Bulat and everybody else. And I've seen people get those certificates to be entered into their world history, so I asked for one, why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Please take a look at the last sentence now: "This certificate is issued at the request of the above-named and is to be used for the purpose of regulating the pensionable service record." Now you're telling that you received this document without so much as looking at it. And I've just read what it says there, that you were the one who actually requested to be issued this document from Colonel Bulat. And then you didn't even look at it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to explain this, Judge. I did take a look at the document. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... are you suggesting I had that in my pocket, that I stamped it myself? I don't get your question. It was given by Mr. Bulat; he was in that building [Interpretation] Mosa Pijade 2, third floor. When I requested this document -- [In English] When I requested this document, he said, Don't worry; I'll give it to you. He gave it to me, and he stamped it. I might have, at the time, assumed that this is a new formation of the government in exile, maybe they have a different name now. What do I know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the witness testified that he did not look at the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. But he said that he did see Colonel Bulat affixing that stamp on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Correct? Did I understand you correctly? When you went to see Colonel Bulat, he signed the document and affixed the stamp on it. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Excellent. Sir, I put it to you that this document is a forgery. So now let me call up document 2D -- 2D37. This is a government conclusion, the conclusion of the Government of the Republic of Serbia. And I will read to you what my request to the government was. My request was to be provided, for the purposes of this trial, by the Ministry of Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. This is a conclusion whereby it says that I -- it is approved. But 2D35 should actually be a reply to my request. Could we please pull up 2D35.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And while we wait for it to come up, let me just tell you that my request was to obtain from the Yugoslav Army information about the chiefs, commanders, of the 40th Personnel Centre of the Yugoslav Army, all their names from the moment of its establishment up until the moment when it was actually dismantled. So you see this here is my request. And now I would like us to take a look at 2D36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before that document is displayed, I would just remind Mr. Bakrac in the document it seems to suggest that Serbia may be seeking protective measures for this document. I'm not what conversations he's had with Serbia, but I don't know whether private session might be required before we display and discuss this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was not my understanding. My understanding was that this document should not be used and may not be used for any other purposes other than for these proceedings. But out of a abundance of caution, we can move on to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, it's your document, apparently. So even if you say out of a abundance of caution, which then assumes a possibility that you may be mistaken in what you earlier said, let's follow, then, that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, you will see in the next document, where I submitted similar requests, they did not provide the information because of the reasons mentioned earlier, the protective measures. So I think I can use this document in open session, but only for the purposes of this trial. So can we now see 2D36, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, here we see the reply to my request, and it says here that Lalic Ljubomir: Father's name, Strahinja, a retired air-force colonel, was appointed between the 1st of July, 1967, to 31st December, 1998, as the chief of the 40th Personnel Centre. And I asked, in other words, to be provided the names of all of the chiefs of this personnel centre, and they provided that name. And that was one name, Ljubomir Lalic, the retired colonel. So my claim here is that either you or Mr. Bulat actually falsified that certificate that you showed me -- showed -- that we showed earlier. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's incorrect on both accounts. I don't think Colonel Bulat falsified it, neither did I. I think it is a genuine document issued by the fall of 1995, beginning of 1996; they decided they were going to make some changes [indiscernible] which they did. I really don't know what it has got to do with me. I mean, it should be beyond any reasonable doubt that I have been there for almost five years. And all I did was ask for somebody to confirm that I was there so I can enter it in my work history book. So what is the problem there?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we -- I would like to tender both of these documents, as well as 2D38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: As these documents were received pursuant to an RFA, there is no objection, Your Honours. But I will point out that 2D38 is already admitted as Prosecution Exhibit 234.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, therefore, there is no need to have that admitted into evidence, from what I understand. Then what remains is 2D37. Is that the one -- the first one. No, 2D36, I think it is. Let me just check. Madam Registrar, the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to understand. D237 was what exactly? That's not what is on our screen at this moment but that was the letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. That's correct. That's the letter, 2D ... 2D37, Your Honours, is the reply or, rather, the conclusion of the Government of the Republic of Serbia approving my request or granting my request and providing the reply as to the identity of the chief of the 40th Personnel Centre; whereas, 2D36 is the reply from which we can see the reply to my request of 16 November, showing who the chief of the 40th Personnel Centre of the Yugoslav Army was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now in evidence already is 2D37? 2D38.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D38 was the OTP exhibit already. It was a P number, so I withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2D36 and 2D37 are admitted into evidence. Under what numbers, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D21 and D22, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D21 and D22 are admitted, therefore. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Could we now please see 65 ter document 535 on the monitors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I read in this document, at least in translation, clearly, that it can be used only to prepare Defence in the proceedings, and it will not be publicly disclosed or used in any other way outside. That's rather ambiguous language. That's -- but I rely on you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm very well aware of it. This is the usual wording used by the bureaucracy. When they say, For use in the preparation of the trial, that is the standard formulation they use. I'm pretty certain of what I'm doing is correct. But I didn't have time to send the document back and ask them to actually correct this, because, as you know, this witness was supposed to come and give evidence in December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, do you recognise this document before you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still have the little ID as a souvenir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who issued this ID to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Rather, this is an official ID?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry. Is this -- did somebody ask me is this an official ID? Yes it was. It was given to me at the station of police in Vojnic by Djuro Skaljac, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, it says here official ID, and then it says the reserve complement; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you say that this was issued by Djuro Skaljac in Vojnic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you take a look, please, at the stamp. It says the Glina SUP, and allegedly it was signed by the minister. I assume that this should have been signed by the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know. All I know is that this was the time when demobilisation was implemented and all of us wake up in the morning being police officers. I know I didn't print it, if this is what you are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now going to ask to see on the left side on the screen for comparison sake, no need for translation, to place on the left side of the screen 2D52.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This document was allegedly issued to you on the 4th of May, 1992. Is this correct? This first one, your official ID in the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. May 4th, 1992. That is correct date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Now can we look at the place here where it says Dusan Pokrajac, the 3rd of March, 1992 -- the 10th of March, 1992, and the minister is signed here, Minister Martic. Is that the same signature as the one on your ID card? You can also look at the first page where it states --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
